meta.title: F4: how power plants turn heat, water, wind and sunlight into electricity (sources, plants, toy settings)
meta.note: Every real number below names its source (sources.*), with where in the document and an as-of date; all were read on 3 November 2026. Prairie Town, its 200 MW solar farm, its combined-cycle plant's 40 MW/h ramp, the hydro plant and its reservoir are illustrative. The solar days are real Southwest Power Pool shapes from town_year.json (EIA-930, 2025), scaled the lesson-0 way: MW = shape x 200 MW, so SPP's highest solar hour of 2025 is the farm at full output. The thermal plants' shares come from EIA's 2025 tested heat rates (3,412 Btu in a kWh / heat rate); the renewable plants' shares are EIA's notional equipment efficiencies (AER 2010, Table F1) and EIA's description of today's best solar modules. The two kinds of number are not measured the same way; the page says so.

eia_t82.title: Electric Power Annual, Table 8.2: Average Tested Heat Rates by Prime Mover and Energy Source, 2015-2025
eia_t82.where: 2025 column; heat rate at full load, weighted by net summer capacity, utilities and independent power producers

eia_faq107.title: Frequently Asked Questions: What is the efficiency of different types of power plants?
eia_faq107.where: divide 3,412 Btu (one kWh) by the heat rate; 10,500 Btu gives 33%, 7,500 Btu gives 45%

eia_gloss.title: Glossary: Heat rate; Heat content
eia_gloss.where: heat rates are typically net heat rates; EIA typically uses gross heat content (higher heating value)

eia_aer2010.title: Annual Energy Review 2010, Appendix F, Table F1: Conversion Efficiencies of Noncombustible Renewable Energy Sources
eia_aer2010.where: p. 358 (Table F1, notional efficiencies: geothermal 16%, conventional hydroelectric 90%, wind 26% at rated wind speed); p. 340 (Table A6, technology-based geothermal heat rate 21,017 Btu per kWh, 2010)

eia_pv.title: Solar explained: Photovoltaics and electricity
eia_pv.where: PV cells are nonmechanical and make direct current; inverters convert it to AC; state-of-the-art modules approach 25% efficiency (under 10% in the mid-1980s)

eia_gen.title: Electricity explained: How electricity is generated
eia_gen.where: most electricity comes from turbines driving generators; shares of U.S. generation in 2022: steam turbines about 42%, combined-cycle plants about 34%, wind turbines about 10%, hydroelectric turbines about 6%, photovoltaic plants about 3%

eia_geo.title: Geothermal explained: Geothermal power plants
eia_geo.where: plants need hot water or steam at 300 to 700 °F; dry steam, flash steam (the most common) and binary-cycle plants; the water is injected back into the ground

eia_hydro.title: Hydropower explained
eia_hydro.where: run-of-river, storage and pumped-storage plants; hydropower about 5.6% of U.S. utility-scale generation in 2025

doe_hydro.publisher: U.S. Department of Energy, Water Power Technologies Office
doe_hydro.title: Types of Hydropower Plants
doe_hydro.where: impoundment (a dam and reservoir, the most common type), diversion (run-of-river) and pumped storage

doe_gas.publisher: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management
doe_gas.title: How Gas Turbine Power Plants Work
doe_gas.where: compressor, combustor (more than 2,000 °F), turbine; a heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) makes steam from the exhaust for a steam turbine; simple-cycle efficiency 20 to 35 percent

eia_startup.title: About 25% of U.S. power plants can start up within an hour
eia_startup.where: Today in Energy: most hydro turbines go from cold start to full output in under 10 minutes; combustion turbines are relatively fast; most combined-cycle plants take 1 to 12 hours; coal plants more than half a day; ramp rate is how fast a running plant changes its output

nrel_dl15.title: Power Performance Test Report for the U.S. Department of Energy 1.5-Megawatt Wind Turbine (NREL/TP-5000-63684)
nrel_dl15.where: Table 6: the highest binned power coefficient, 0.52 at 7.04 m/s (lesson 5's data file)

scenes.name: Gas plant
scenes.spins: A gas turbine, then (in a combined cycle) a steam turbine
scenes.text: Burning gas drives a [[gas-turbine|gas turbine]] like a jet engine. A combined cycle also boils water with the hot exhaust, so a second, [[steam-turbine|steam turbine]] runs on heat the peaker throws away.

scenes.name: Steam plant
scenes.energy: Coal or gas burned in a boiler (or heat from fission: F5)
scenes.text: A boiler turns water into steam that spins a steam turbine. A [[condenser|condenser]] cools the steam back to water, and that is where most of the [[waste-heat|waste heat]] leaves.

scenes.name: Hydro dam
scenes.text: A dam holds a [[reservoir|reservoir]]. Water falls through a pipe, the penstock, and spins a turbine; the drop in height is the [[hydraulic-head|head]].

scenes.name: Geothermal plant
scenes.energy: Hot water or steam from wells, 300 to 700 °F
chain: Hot water rises in a well
Steam flashes and spins a turbine
scenes.text: [[geothermal|Geothermal]] wells bring up hot water under pressure; at the surface part of it flashes to steam that spins a turbine. The cooled water goes back down another well.

scenes.name: Wind turbine
scenes.spins: The rotor, then a generator in the nacelle
scenes.text: The wind turns the blades, and the rotor turns a [[generator|generator]] in the nacelle on top of the tower. No rotor can catch more than 59.3% of the wind's power (the Betz limit, lesson 5).

scenes.name: Solar photovoltaic farm
scenes.text: [[photovoltaic|Photovoltaic]] cells turn light straight into direct current, with nothing spinning. An [[inverter|inverter]] turns it into the grid's alternating current.

pv1985.note: commercial panels averaged less than 10% in the mid-1980s

solar.pickNote: Picked on 3 November 2026 from the SPP solar shape of 27 August to 14 September 2025 (similar day length). 11 September has the most solar energy among those days whose hour from 19:00 stays at or below a quarter of the day's peak (12 September holds its peak through that hour, a likely telemetry error, so it is left out); 5 September has the least solar energy of June to September; 3 September is lesson 0's day.

hydro.about: Illustrative plant. Power P = rho x g x Q x H x eta (W), in MW / 1e6. The reservoir holds 20 million cubic metres of usable water (illustrative); at a flow Q it runs for volume / (Q x 3600) hours.

ramp.about: Prairie Town's 3 September 2025, prepared exactly as in lesson 0 (grid-operator.js prepare): the gas each hour must supply, 15:00 to 21:00. The combined-cycle plant follows that need as closely as its ramp limit and size allow (greedy, hour by hour), starting from the need at 15:00; the peaker fills what is missing, up to its size. The ramp limit slider is illustrative; Prairie Town's own plant is 40 MW per hour (town.json).

cards.text: A cloud bank crosses the solar farm at noon
cards.why: Weather: a solar farm can make only what the sunlight allows.

cards.text: A calm night: the wind farm's blades barely turn
cards.why: Weather: a wind farm can make only what the wind allows.

cards.text: After a dry year, the dam's reservoir is low
cards.why: Stored water: the head and the hours of full output both shrink.

cards.text: A gas pipeline is shut for repair
cards.why: Fuel: a gas plant can run only while gas arrives.

cards.text: Demand climbs 50 MW in an hour; the combined-cycle plant can add only 40 MW
cards.why: Ramp rate: the plant has room to give more, just not that fast.
